operator_plays.name: New-LLC & Recorded-Deed Trigger-Mail Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Ingest daily Secretary of State new-LLC filings and County Recorder new-deed/mortgage recordings to trigger programmatic direct mail via API—replacing illegal government-lookalike poster/deed invoices (which violate 39 U.S.C. § 3001 and state deed-solicitation laws) with high-LTV recurring workplace compliance subscriptions, property-tax appeal contingency offers, and exclusive new-mover/B2B lead monetization.
inputs: Daily Secretary of State new-entity (LLC/Corp) bulk feeds
County Recorder grant/warranty deed & mortgage recording dockets
Programmatic print-and-mail API (Lob / PostGrid) + QR intake bridge
workflow: Pull daily new-LLC formations (filtering for employer/commercial NAICS or multi-member filings) and newly recorded residential deeds with purchase price and loan metadata
Dispatch transparent, non-governmental trigger mailers within 24–48 hours of filing with personalized QR codes pre-populating entity or parcel data

Monetize new LLCs via recurring annual labor-poster/registered-agent compliance memberships and B2B partner referrals; monetize new deeds via contingency property-tax appeal filings or high-ticket homeowner lead sales
metrics: Filing-to-mailbox latency (hours)
QR scan & intake conversion % per 1,000 mailers
Annualized LTV / net revenue per mailed piece

platform_risks.failure_mode: USPS 39 U.S.C. § 3001(h)-(i) mail-stop order, State AG UDAP enforcement, or payment-processor freeze
platform_risks.trigger: Styling mailers as fake government penalty notices, invoices, or charging $89-$195 solely for a $3 public deed copy without statutory disclaimers
platform_risks.impact: Civil restitution penalties, merchant account termination, and 30%+ chargeback rates
platform_risks.detection_metric: Refund/chargeback ratio >1% and customer support inquiries mistaking the mailer for a government agency
platform_risks.fallback: Use unambiguous private commercial branding, never mimic government seals or citation numbers, and sell genuine value-add subscriptions (annual compliance updates, tax-assessment appeals, or B2B services)

operator_plays.name: Arizona ABS Law-Firm Ownership & Survivor/Mass-Tort Co-Counsel Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Leverage Arizona Supreme Court Rule 31.1(c) and ACJA § 7-209 (which abolished ABA Rule 5.4 in Arizona via Alternative Business Structure [ABS] licensing) so non-lawyer acquisition operators can legally own an Arizona law firm, acquire inbound institutional sexual assault survivor claims (juvenile detention facilities, rideshare MDLs, clergy/boarding-school/medical lookback windows) and catastrophic mass torts, and participate in lawful co-counsel contingency fee splits ($50k–$400k+ per settled case) instead of capped flat marketing fees.
inputs: Arizona Supreme Court ABS license + designated Compliance Lawyer (ACJA § 7-209)
Trauma-informed inbound acquisition funnels for state sexual-assault lookback windows & federal MDLs
24/7 HIPAA-compliant survivor intake, facility/ride-receipt verification, & national trial co-counsel network
workflow: Form or partner with a licensed Arizona ABS law firm with an appointed Arizona-bar Compliance Lawyer to legally bridge digital acquisition and legal representation
Run empathetic, 100% inbound survivor-advocacy campaigns across open statutory lookback windows (juvenile detention centers, Uber/Lyft rideshare MDL 3084, institutional/youth-facility abuse)

Execute trauma-informed intake, verify facility/detention/rideshare records, and co-counsel with specialized trial litigators under Rule 1.5(e) joint-responsibility agreements to share in back-end settlement fees
metrics: Cost per signed & record-verified survivor retainer ($1,200–$3,500 media cost)
Facility/rideshare corroboration pass rate (%) & zero-fraud docket quality
Realized co-counsel contingency fee per settled case ($50,000–$400,000+ vs. $3k lead sale)

platform_risks.failure_mode: Cross-jurisdictional Rule 5.4 fee-splitting challenges, MDL claimant-fraud rejections, or 24–48 month settlement lockup
platform_risks.trigger: Splitting fees in non-ABS jurisdictions without genuine legal services/joint responsibility by ABS attorneys, accepting unverified lead-brokered retainers, or undercapitalizing multi-year MDL hold times
platform_risks.impact: Disallowance of co-counsel fee division in restrictive states, court dismissal of uncorroborated claims, or working-capital exhaustion before settlement payout
platform_risks.detection_metric: 100% primary-record corroboration rate (detention/medical/ride logs) and state-by-state Rule 1.5(e)/5.4 ethics opinion sign-off
platform_risks.fallback: Ensure licensed ABS attorneys perform substantive legal intake/case-work or pair with an MSO (Management Services Organization) structure in restrictive states, enforce strict primary-document verification before filing, and blend fast-settling single-event injury cases with multi-year institutional dockets

Location-consistent EXIF metadata, mobile device telemetry, and verifiable third-party citation dossiers
B2B local-SEO, knowledge-graph, and SaaS launch client demand

Use high-tier Local Guide accounts to submit rapid-approval GBP spam-name redressals, competitor duplicate merges, and category corrections for local-service clients
Execute policy-compliant, source-backed knowledge-graph updates and high-visibility Product Hunt/directory launches for B2B SaaS brands
Package these high-trust authority interventions as premium reputation, entity-SEO, and launch-management retainers ($2,500–$10,000/mo)

Client local-pack rank lift or knowledge-panel entity resolution rate (%)

operator_plays.mechanism: Provisioning hundreds of isolated secondary domains across subsidized Microsoft 365 developer/partner tenants, Cloudflare Email Routing, and low-cost SMTP relays—sending strictly 15–25 plain-text emails per inbox per day across 300+ free/subsidized mailboxes to deliver 150,000+ monthly B2B cold emails into primary inboxes without paying $6–$12/seat retail Google Workspace pricing.
inputs: Lookalike secondary domain portfolio with automated SPF, DKIM (2048-bit), DMARC (`p=quarantine`/`reject`), and custom tracking-free MX records
Subsidized M365 partner/developer tenants, Cloudflare Email Routing catch-alls, and distributed SMTP sending nodes
Automated peer-to-peer warmup network and master unibox reply-routing webhook
workflow: Provision 100–300 secondary sending domains and bind 2–3 mailboxes per domain via automated DNS and tenant scripts
Warm every mailbox for 14–21 days with realistic thread-depth conversations before introducing live outbound prospects
Cap daily outbound volume at <=20 zero-link, zero-tracking-pixel plain-text messages per mailbox per day to stay completely beneath ESP volume heuristics
Aggregate all prospect replies into a single unified AI-triaged inbox that books qualified B2B sales calls on pay-per-show or retainer terms

All-in monthly infrastructure cost per 10,000 delivered plain-text emails ($)
Positive reply rate (%) and booked meetings per 1,000 prospects contacted

platform_risks.failure_mode: Tenant-wide outbound throttling or domain-footprint blacklisting (Spamhaus DBL)
platform_risks.trigger: Placing too many domains inside a single tenant, embedding tracking pixels, or exceeding 30 sends/day per mailbox
platform_risks.impact: Tenant suspension or domain-level spam-folder routing
platform_risks.detection_metric: Daily seed-list inbox placement (%) and bounce rate (<1.5% hard threshold)

operator_plays.name: Wholesale Telecom Voice Traffic Pumping, 8YY Toll-Free & A2P SMS Termination Arbitrage

inputs: Revenue-share interconnect agreements with licensed CLECs, tandem switches, or international SMS aggregators
Ranges of high-yield DIDs, 8YY toll-free numbers, or international mobile virtual numbers (LVNs)
Free high-duration consumer voice utilities (AI companion hotlines, diaspora radio/prayer lines, conference bridges, OTP test/verification tools)

Promote free, high-retention voice or messaging services that organically drive millions of inbound call minutes or A2P verification messages
Route inbound traffic through compliant SIP trunks to the terminating carrier switch and log CDR (Call Detail Record) duration and completion telemetry
Collect contractual revenue-share rebates (30–65% of intercarrier settlement receipts) on settled carrier invoices every 30–45 days
metrics: Monthly settled inbound minutes of use (MOU) and A2P SMS termination volume
Effective net rebate per minute ($0.004–$0.03) or per international SMS ($0.02–$0.12)
Originating-carrier dispute/withholding rate (%) across settlement cycles

platform_risks.impact: Tandem/end-office tariff step-down to bill-and-keep or carrier billing dispute freezes
platform_risks.detection_metric: Per-OCN inbound/outbound traffic ratio and zero synthetic/auto-dialed CDR patterns
platform_risks.fallback: Distribute traffic across multiple global jurisdictions and non-access-stimulation SIP monetization models, and require 100% genuine human user initiation with STIR/SHAKEN attestation

operator_plays.name: White-Label MVNO & Federal/State Low-Income Telecom Subsidy Aggregation
operator_plays.mechanism: Launching a white-label Mobile Virtual Network Operator (MVNO) or partnering as a master enrollment aggregator for Eligible Telecommunications Carriers (ETCs) to enroll hundreds of thousands of SNAP/Medicaid/SSI-eligible households into '100% Free Unlimited Talk/Text/Data' plans—arbitraging the spread between $2–$4/mo wholesale MVNO network COGS and $9.25–$44+/mo in combined Federal Lifeline, Tribal, and State (e.g., California LifeLine) monthly government reimbursements.

National Verifier (USAC NLAD) API integration checking SNAP, Medicaid, WIC, and SSI eligibility in real time
Omnichannel street-team tablet canopy network and geotargeted digital co-registration funnels in high-subsidy zip codes

Verify applicant eligibility instantly against the USAC National Verifier / state administrator API and provision an instant eSIM or pre-activated pSIM
Pay enrollment agents or digital media channels a $15–$35 one-time acquisition bounty while collecting recurring monthly government reimbursements ($15–$44+/mo) plus upsold data top-ups
Automate 30-day usage heartbeats (outbound call/SMS check-ins) so enrolled lines satisfy mandatory USAC monthly active-usage rules
metrics: Active reimbursed subscriber base and monthly net ARPU ($12–$38/mo) vs. wholesale carrier COGS ($2.50–$4.50/mo)
30-day USAC non-usage de-enrollment ('cure') rate (%)
Customer acquisition cost (CAC) payback period (target: <45 days)

platform_risks.failure_mode: USAC audit clawback for duplicate household enrollments or 30-day non-usage de-enrollment rules
platform_risks.trigger: Field agents enrolling ineligible subscribers or lines going 30 consecutive days without an outbound call, text, or data session
platform_risks.impact: Mandatory de-enrollment of inactive lines or USAC reimbursement recoupment
platform_risks.detection_metric: Rolling 20-day zero-usage cohort alerts and 100% NLAD/National Verifier API pre-check enforcement
platform_risks.fallback: Run automated Day-20 SMS/IVR engagement campaigns ('Reply YES to keep your free monthly service active') and strictly claw back field-agent commissions on any line failing 30-day usage

operator_plays.name: Employer Self-Funded ERISA Plan International Specialty-Drug Importation Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Contracting with mid-market US employers (100–5,000 employees) operating self-funded ERISA health plans to carve out high-cost specialty biologics and GLP-1s ($6,000–$15,000/mo US PBM list price) and source the identical manufacturer-sealed drugs from licensed Tier-1 pharmacies in Canada, the UK, Australia, and New Zealand at $800–$2,200/mo—waiving the employee's copay to $0 while taking 25–35% of the employer's $50,000–$100,000/yr per-patient savings.
inputs: Department of Labor (DOL) Form 5500 Schedule A/C database identifying self-funded ERISA employers by broker, TPA, and stop-loss carrier
Licensed international pharmacy dispensation network across Tier-1 jurisdictions (Canada, UK, Australia, New Zealand) with cold-chain courier logistics
Turnkey ERISA Summary Plan Description (SPD) 'Specialty Drug Carve-Out Amendment' and $0-copay patient concierge portal

Audit the employer's anonymized pharmacy claims file to flag the 1–3% of members driving 45–60% of total drug spend (Humira, Stelara, Skyrizi, Dupixent, Enbrel, Ozempic)
Plug in a voluntary $0-copay international personal-importation program alongside the existing TPA, fulfilling 90-day cold-chain prescriptions at 60–80% below US PBM prices
Bill the self-funded employer plan a shared-savings contingency fee equal to 25–35% of verified net claim reduction ($15,000–$30,000/yr per enrolled specialty patient)
metrics: Verified annual specialty-claim savings ($) per self-funded employer group
Net shared-savings fee revenue ($15k–$30k/yr) per enrolled specialty patient
Employee $0-copay opt-in conversion rate (target: >85%)

operator_plays.name: 340B Contract-Pharmacy & Covered-Entity Drug Price Spread Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Partnering with HRSA-qualified 340B Covered Entities (Federally Qualified Health Centers, Ryan White clinics, disproportionate-share rural hospitals) to provide turnkey Third-Party Administrator (TPA) split-billing software, specialty contract-pharmacy fulfillment, and tele-referral capture—buying outpatient specialty medications at 25–50%+ statutory 340B discounts while collecting 100% full commercial insurance reimbursement and splitting the multi-thousand-dollar per-script margin via compliant flat administrative/dispensing fees.

340B split-billing / virtual-inventory accumulator software tracking 11-digit NDCs, prescriber NPIs, and patient-eligibility encounters
Licensed specialty/mail-order contract pharmacy network and commercial payer PBMs

Deploy split-billing TPA software and mail-order specialty contract-pharmacy infrastructure that captures commercially insured prescriptions written or co-managed by clinic providers
Reimburse the pharmacy at full commercial payer rates ($3,000–$12,000/script) while replenishing drug inventory via the clinic's 340B wholesaler account at $800–$4,000/script
Charge fixed fair-market-value per-dispense administrative, software, and clinical-management fees that capture a major share of the net spread while funding the clinic's safety-net mission

Gross commercial-to-340B acquisition spread ($1,500–$6,000+) per specialty fill
HRSA audit pass rate (zero duplicate Medicaid discount or diversion findings)

operator_plays.name: Out-of-Network DME, CGM & Diagnostic Reference Lab Billing Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Operating a healthcare Management Services Organization (MSO) and performance patient-acquisition engine that pairs targeted paid-social symptom funnels with independent telehealth physician groups and licensed Durable Medical Equipment (DME) / reference lab suppliers—acquiring insured patients at $85–$220 CAC for high-margin HCPCS/CPT codes (Continuous Glucose Monitors, pneumatic compression devices, home sleep testing, custom orthotics) that reimburse $900–$3,500+ against $70–$220 hardware COGS.

Real-time insurance-eligibility and deductible verification API (Availity / Waystar / Stedi)
Compliant Management Services Organization (MSO) software + flat-fee marketing contracts with PECOS-enrolled DME suppliers and telehealth PCs

First-pass clean claim acceptance rate (%) and days sales outstanding (DSO)
Physician medical-necessity chart audit pass rate (100% LCD/NCD criteria match)

chapters.question_prompt: How do we define best-fit buyers, research their problems, and choose routes into commercial and federal markets?
chapters.title: Define the Buyer and the Route to Market
chapters.subtitle: Problem-led ICPs, customer research, buyer personas, qualification scorecards, customer clusters, B2B sales stages, pipeline-focused agencies, and federal notices and teaming partners
chapters.executive_summary: The practitioners converge on one rule: define the buyer by the pain you fix, then cut the market until only accounts with active, budgeted, urgent pain remain. OGONJO Workbooks, Myk Pono and Connor Murray all build targeting from problems and outcomes rather than products or titles, while The Influence, WebFX and Misar AI put the company-level ICP filter ahead of persona work. The street mechanics are tight. Hunter's 31M-email data shows lists of 100 or fewer more than double replies. OGONJO scores 5 to 7 criteria and disqualifies 20 to 30%, and Dan Martell trims 50,000 accounts to 800 with technographics. The disagreements run on list size and route to market: Hunter's 50-to-100-person sequences against Jeff Borshawa's 10-to-12 whales, sales-led against marketing-led on Prairie Founders Club's $10K LTV line, and Neil McDonnell's federal notice-and-teaming path.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every serious operator here starts targeting from the pain, not the product. OGONJO Workbooks puts it bluntly: stop defining your company by what you do and define it by what you fix. A customer buys a solution to a problem, not a product, and each seat feels that problem differently. The CFO feels cost, the VP of Sales feels lost revenue, and the end user feels frustration [ZSqgCrydlAo @ 00:00:30]. Myk Pono runs the same logic as a funnel. The target audience is everyone who has the pain. Potential customers add fit and budget, meaning more than 25 employees or over $1M ARR. The true ICP is the slice where that pain is active and they are already looking for a solution [Y1u-ngsyH60 @ 00:01:46]. Connor Murray narrows in a fixed order of territory, then ICP, then accounts, then people. He prioritizes by industry, company size, use case, and the business outcomes and KPIs the buyer is measured on [DBGq--oFsQ8 @ 00:01:20]. Hunter's team adds a hard three-part test: a target must have hair-on-fire pain, budget and authority, and a message you can actually tailor to them. Miss any one of the three and the account drops out [35H3HVb8ymw @ 00:16:35]. The shared operating rule is that if you cannot state the pain in the buyer's own words, you do not have an ICP yet. You have a product description pointed at a crowd.

The second point of agreement is that a smaller, sharper list beats volume. Hunter's state-of-email-outreach data, built on 31M outreach emails, shows that lists of 100 leads or fewer more than double replies. Meanwhile, 61% of decision makers call most outreach irrelevant, because a bigger audience forces a broader, weaker message [35H3HVb8ymw @ 00:09:28]. lemlist frames the same trap in one line: reaching out to everybody means reaching nobody [7hSBNM6xnmc @ 00:00:12]. Jeff Borshawa, on Marketing in the Age of AI, takes it to the extreme. You need 10 to 12 people, not 30,000, and treating suspects as prospects is the core mistake. Ten, maybe 20, ideal clients will change a small business's trajectory. Jeff ties this whale-hunting approach to Chad Holmes's Dream 100 and a granular top-100 list, and warns that chasing minnows means small deals that carry no margin [M-Z0SPYJ9-w @ 00:19:38]. Dan Martell explains why focus compounds with the image of air pressure in a tire. A tight geographic focus builds a mini-brand: LA for music, New York and Bay Street for finance, the Midwest for farm [RqN41GVY6UQ @ 00:01:30]. Across the board, the operators treat narrowing as the lever that raises response, not as a cap on upside. Spray-and-pray signals such as a 10,000-name list, or the complaint that outreach just doesn't work, are the tell that the target is wrong.

The third consensus is that the ICP is a company-level filter that runs before any persona work, and its real job is to cut. The Influence opens with a cautionary case: perfect personas sitting inside companies that could not afford the product. It lands on a fixed order, with the ICP first as the filter and the persona second to personalize. In their words, the ICP tells you which doors to knock on and the persona tells you exactly what to say when somebody answers [_i5Xkz85mPA @ 00:04:59]. WebFX draws the identical split. The ICP is company traits and the persona is a fictional individual such as 'Sally, 54.' Both should be specific enough to name northern Kansas counties and a 20-to-90-employee band [V7x_5WjVUiw @ 00:00:57]. OGONJO Workbooks calls the ICP a disqualification tool outright and warns that a vague ICP is worse than having none at all [4S63IHiDhTk @ 00:01:07]. Misar AI builds that cutting power straight into the worksheet. Every row is one filter that exports to the CRM, and anti-ICP rows sit beside the positives as hard negatives: commodity manufacturing, low budget, no CRM [giIGT_MMd5k @ 00:01:58]. The working stack has two layers. Fit decides whether an account gets touched at all, and only then does the persona shape the words, the KPIs you speak to, and the sign-off authority you need to reach.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Hunter's build is the most concrete. Skip TAM, SAM and SOM for outreach, which Matt calls terrible for this job. Work in the obtainable ring instead and pick the segment you can dominate, where buyers are desperate [35H3HVb8ymw @ 00:12:15]. Their Proposely example shows the precision expected: marketing and creative agencies with 10 to 15 employees, US-based, founded 2015 to 2022. Seed the search with your 10 to 20 best customers and run the funnel from market to company to person. Stop at 50 to 80 people, maybe 100. The validation check is that existing customers start showing up in your filters. Matt filters on headcount, not revenue, except for AI companies, because there is no good revenue data on any company that does not publish it [35H3HVb8ymw @ 00:28:02]. In the live Discover AI demo, natural-language search took roughly 2,000 companies down to 337 people and then to 44 in California. Dan Martell runs the same compression on technographics. He mines BuiltWith and job posts for tech-stack clues and trims 50,000 accounts to 800 [RqN41GVY6UQ @ 00:03:24]. Misar AI's SaaS worksheet lands in a similar range: UK, Germany and France, 100 to 500 employees, $10M to $50M ARR, running AWS plus Zapier. It targets a Head of Ops or VP Product and yields 150 to 200 accounts [giIGT_MMd5k @ 00:03:03].

Once the list exists, the practitioners score it and hunt for timing. OGONJO Workbooks wants a one-sentence ICP statement backed by 5 to 7 criteria scored 0 to 5, including the health of the decision-making unit. Their benchmark is to disqualify 20 to 30% of opportunities and see roughly a three-times win-rate gap between high and low scorers. Their cybersecurity case used three criteria: revenue above $100M, a regulated industry, and a named security officer. It lifted SDR productivity 45% and acceptance 35% [4S63IHiDhTk @ 00:04:33]. For timing, Hunter's Matt points to hiring, funding, tech-stack and social signals. He warns to wait a couple of weeks after a new HR hire before pitching, since only 2 to 8% of any market is actively looking at a given moment [35H3HVb8ymw @ 00:32:17]. lemlist converts the persona into a scrapable persona for LinkedIn filters. SDR headcount growth signals revenue goals, and a years-in-position filter tightens the cut further [7hSBNM6xnmc @ 00:04:48]. Misar AI applies negative filters first: competitor partners, data-law noncompliance and integration gaps. Only then does it layer SIC and NAICS codes, refreshing the list weekly [giIGT_MMd5k @ 00:06:39]. The net mechanic is to score, time and exclude before a single email goes out, so the send budget is spent only on accounts that clear every gate.

The route to market is where the numbers get specific. Hunter's sending rules start with a 15-per-day floor and a cap around 200 to 250 against a roughly 500 provider limit, with a recommendation of 50 or fewer per day. Run one sequence per quarter at 3 to 4 steps, and remember that progressive sending is not warm-up [35H3HVb8ymw @ 00:51:28]. If you are sitting on 10,000 leads, split them into ten lists of 1,000 using one or two levers. Prairie Founders Club picks the motion with a 2x2 of B2B versus B2C and LTV over or under $10K. B2B above $10K is sales-led and B2C below $10K is marketing-led. LTV is total revenue divided by total customers, calculated on at least three years of data [VJjRWz_6Hq0 @ 00:02:08]. On paid, GrowthSpree, pitching its own $3,000-a-month flat model, argues that the tell is the feedback loop. Feed tiered CRM conversions back to Google, LinkedIn and Meta: MQL at $100, SQL at $900, opportunity at $3,000, closed-won at deal value. Their reasoning is that only 13% of MQLs become SQL [YOYPAYz4iOc @ 00:02:44]. For the federal route, Neil McDonnell treats SAM.gov, DIBBS, Unison, GSA eBuy and CPORT as a daily exercise, and his SAM walkthrough filtered 3,800 notices to 1,000 and then to 177 [YL3LT_x34Ms @ 00:21:57].

callout.title: Small moves the operators use to sharpen targeting and reply rates
callout.body: These are the low-effort adjustments the practitioners call out as outsized: widen contacts inside an account, dig to the emotional driver, build rooms instead of pitching them, and settle money before paperwork.
items: Email more than one person per target company. Hunter's outreach data shows almost +50% replies, and editing templates plus body personalization adds about another +50% [Hunter — 35H3HVb8ymw @ 00:10:21].
Run the Five Whys on every problem statement, asking 'why does that matter?' five times until you hit the emotional reason the buyer will act [OGONJO Workbooks — ZSqgCrydlAo @ 00:08:35].

Instead of pitching widgets at conferences, where only about 3% are in market, host virtual networking groups and deliberately stack the room with your ICP [Marketing in the Age of AI — M-Z0SPYJ9-w @ 00:16:06].

Talk rates before signing the teaming agreement. A partner charging $200 against your $100 will break the bid, so one way or another you have to talk about rates early [Neil McDonnell — d_oQ5UhlC0k @ 00:20:28].

sop_steps.title: Pin down the problem you fix
sop_steps.action: Mine call notes, support tickets and surveys for the top three problems, then pick the most urgent as the core statement.
sop_steps.detail: Write the problem in the customer's words, cascade it to the C-suite, department head and end user, and get a gut check from a sales colleague; target 1 to 2 problem statements in circulation [OGONJO Workbooks — ZSqgCrydlAo @ 00:03:13].

sop_steps.title: Clone your most profitable clients
sop_steps.action: Pull roughly your 10 most profitable clients and extract shared firmographic, technographic, cultural and recent-change attributes.
sop_steps.detail: Use BuiltWith for tech stack, interview customers directly, then prioritize 5 to 10 attributes such as ready, urgent, willing, able and advocacy potential [lemlist — 7hSBNM6xnmc @ 00:01:25].

sop_steps.title: Write the one-sentence ICP and scorecard
sop_steps.action: Compress the attributes into one sentence backed by 5 to 7 criteria scored 0 to 5, including decision-making-unit health.
sop_steps.detail: Pair firmographic and technographic data with an outcomes framework, avoid 20-point scorecards, and confirm the scorecard disqualifies 20 to 30% of deals [OGONJO Workbooks — 4S63IHiDhTk @ 00:03:24].

sop_steps.title: Build the list and sequence it
sop_steps.action: Seed the search with 10 to 20 best customers, apply excludes, and stop at 50 to 80, maybe 100, people per list.
sop_steps.detail: Exclude wrong industry, contract lock-in and sanctioned locations, then run one 3-to-4-step sequence per quarter at 50 or fewer sends per day [Hunter — 35H3HVb8ymw @ 00:38:43].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first split is where the definition starts. The Influence runs company-first: the ICP is the 'where' filter built from size, revenue above $2M, industry, location, tech stack and urgency such as a compliance deadline, and only after that filter does the persona layer decide what to say [_i5Xkz85mPA @ 00:04:11]. Myk Pono attacks the persona-first habit directly, warning that companies who jump in to create personas miss whole segments, and replaces it with a funnel: target audience is everyone with the pain, potential customers add fit and budget such as more than 25 employees or more than $1M ARR, and the ICP is only the slice whose pain is active and who are already looking for a solution [Y1u-ngsyH60 @ 00:00:47]. OGONJO Workbooks starts further upstream still, arguing a customer buys a solution to a problem, not a product, and cascading one urgent problem statement down to the CFO who feels cost, the VP of Sales who feels lost revenue and the end user who feels frustration before any firmographic row gets written [ZSqgCrydlAo @ 00:00:30]. Prairie Founders Club pushes deepest into the individual, logging hobbies and TV habits because people buy from those they like and trust [VJjRWz_6Hq0 @ 00:04:53].

The second fight is over whether to mine your existing book. lemlist tells operators to pick roughly the 10 most profitable clients and extract shared firmographics, technographics, culture and recent changes, then prioritize 5 to 10 attributes including ready, urgent, willing, able, acquisition efficiency, ascension and advocacy potential [7hSBNM6xnmc @ 00:01:25], and Jeff Borshawa on Marketing in the Age of AI says to look inside your 10 favorite clients and clone them because they already know your next favorite clients [M-Z0SPYJ9-w @ 00:20:55]. The counter-camp is loud. Myk Pono warns that analyzing only the highest-ASP or highest-LTV accounts reinforces the segments you already have, so other segments must be researched proactively [Y1u-ngsyH60 @ 00:02:42]. OGONJO Workbooks calls 'all our current customers' a backward-looking map and defines SOM as only what you can win in the next 12 months [bVYYwxZZ4dU @ 00:05:19]. OGONJO's own answer is to rank 3 to 4 segments, add a technographic layer, and commit 80% of effort to two verticals, which is how a procurement SaaS focused on US SaaS firms with 200 to 1,000 employees on Salesforce plus NetSuite lifted marketing ROI 50% and lead-to-opportunity 30%.

The third split is about sizing the hunt. Hunter's team calls TAM, SAM and SOM terrible for outreach and builds inside a prioritized obtainable market where buyers are desperate, landing on 50 to 80, maybe 100, people per campaign and using headcount over revenue, except for AI companies, because there's no good revenue data about any company that doesn't publish it [35H3HVb8ymw @ 00:12:15]. Jeff Borshawa compresses harder, arguing you need 10 to 12 people, not 30,000, and that 10, maybe 20, ideal clients change a small business's trajectory [M-Z0SPYJ9-w @ 00:19:38]. On deal size, Dan Martell says start low or mid-market and move up, and uses a geography focus to build a mini-brand the way air pressure works in a tire [RqN41GVY6UQ @ 00:01:30]. Martell's technographic trim, using BuiltWith and job-post mining, cuts 50,000 accounts to 800. Jeff runs the opposite play, whale hunting rather than chasing minnows because big players' little problems carry decent budgets while small players' big problems have tiny ones. OGONJO Workbooks then contradicts Martell's geography lever, calling geography-only segments a trap and testing focus by whether a team can put 80% of effort into two verticals [bVYYwxZZ4dU @ 00:05:50].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most repeated failure is aiming at everyone. Hunter's team lists the warning signs verbatim, a list of 10,000 or a hundred thousand and a founder saying outreach just doesn't work, then backs it with data from 31M emails: 61% of decision makers call most outreach irrelevant, a bigger audience forces a broader message, and lists of 100 leads or less more than double replies [35H3HVb8ymw @ 00:06:23]. lemlist frames the same trap as reaching out to everybody and reaching nobody [7hSBNM6xnmc @ 00:00:12]. Jeff Borshawa learned it coaching accounting firms, where general terms produced general results until the framing tightened to three to five partners and 10 to 20 staff; they also reject 'I serve everyone' using skincare's everyone-with-skin pitch as the example [M-Z0SPYJ9-w @ 00:05:13]. The conference variant is worse: at Nvidia GTC with about 30,000 attendees, only 3% are in market, a super connector meets no more than 500 people, the energy lasts 48 to 72 hours then goes quiet for 362 days, and closing a widget pitch there is dumb luck. GrowthSpree adds the downstream symptom, MQLs rising and CPL falling while pipeline stays flat, with only 13% of MQLs becoming SQL [YOYPAYz4iOc @ 00:00:36].

The second trap is mistaking a good-looking target for a buyer. The Influence opens on a cautionary case of perfect personas sitting inside companies that could not afford the product, and treats spreadsheet-run tech stacks as a sign a company is not ready [_i5Xkz85mPA @ 00:00:14]. OGONJO Workbooks says a vague ICP is worse than none, warns against 20-point scorecards and scorecards that just validate the existing pipeline, and sets the bar at 5 to 7 criteria scored 0 to 5, disqualifying 20 to 30% with roughly a three-times win-rate gap between high and low scores [4S63IHiDhTk @ 00:02:18]. Connor Murray carries the trap into the deal: it is very easy to get happy ears, intent is not execution, and in their example legal takes 6 weeks and security another 2, so you can't take anything for granted [DBGq--oFsQ8 @ 00:06:22]. Connor also admits 'I certainly made this mistake when I was new' in negotiation, which is why they insist on knowing discount bands and approval limits beforehand and trading any discount for a longer term, faster decision or upfront payment. GrowthSpree flags the measurement trap: dark-funnel touches get marked direct and under-credited, and the tell is whether tiered CRM values feed back: MQL $100, SQL $900, opportunity $3,000, closed-won at deal value [YOYPAYz4iOc @ 00:02:44].

The economics checks are blunt. Emanuel Rose warns that tiny contracts carry no margin while clients still expect $50,000-a-month results, because a project costs the same to spool up at any size [M-Z0SPYJ9-w @ 00:03:20]. Prairie Founders Club draws the line at $10,000 lifetime value: B2B above it is sales-led, B2C below it is marketing-led, and LTV is total revenue divided by total customers using at least 3 years of data [VJjRWz_6Hq0 @ 00:02:08]. In federal teaming, Neil McDonnell says one way or another you have to talk about rates early, flags a partner charging $200 against your $100 as the conflict to raise before signing the teaming agreement, warns about large primes demanding 49% of workshare, and runs a 1-to-5 requirements gap analysis per subtask where you prime only at an average of 4 and a score of 5 needs 3 past performances [d_oQ5UhlC0k @ 00:20:54]. Hunter's team caps the outbound engine too: a 15-per-day floor, a ceiling around 200 to 250 against a roughly 500 provider limit, a recommendation of 50 or fewer per day, and a reminder that progressive sending is not warm-up [35H3HVb8ymw @ 00:51:28]. They also say to wait a couple of weeks after an HR hire signal before reaching out.

callout.title: Kill the Build Before It Burns Budget
callout.body: Every gate below comes from a practitioner who watched lists, scorecards, deals or partnerships fail on these exact points. Clear all four before scaling sends or signing paper.
items: Never push one message to a 10,000-lead list; split it into 10 x 1,000 segments using one or two levers and keep each sending box at 50 or fewer per day [Hunter — 35H3HVb8ymw @ 00:48:20].

Run the ICP scorecard against open deals and disqualify 20 to 30%; a strong ICP should show roughly a three-times win-rate difference between high and low scores [OGONJO Workbooks — 4S63IHiDhTk @ 00:07:53].
Before any POV, pilot or trial, agree use cases, requirements, people, timeline and success KPIs up front and time-box it at 2 or 4 weeks [Connor Murray — DBGq--oFsQ8 @ 00:11:19].
Prime a federal bid only when the requirements gap analysis averages 4, and settle partner rates before the teaming agreement is signed [Neil McDonnell — d_oQ5UhlC0k @ 00:24:39].

chapters.question_prompt: When should we use account-based marketing, and how do we organize sales, marketing, advertising, and outreach around selected accounts?
chapters.title: Build the Account-Based Marketing Operating System
chapters.subtitle: ABM versus demand generation, high-value account targeting, sales–marketing alignment, LinkedIn, ABM advertising, Claude-assisted outreach, and enterprise pipeline workflows
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners converge on one rule: ABM is a joint sales-and-marketing operating system aimed at a short, tiered account list, not a lead-volume campaign. TK Kader, AdConversion and Fullfunnel io all gate entry on deal size, with floors cited at roughly $20,000 ACV, CFO sign-off, or 30K ACV, and flag a thousand-account list or a $1M-in-30-days expectation as red flags. The street mechanics run ICP, messaging, a Dream 100, personalization, then sales outbound under paid and organic air cover, tracked in weekly account-level meetings. Reported numbers include terminus's 124% demo-to-close lift, Snowflake's 2-3% account-ad click-through against 0.09% display, and a 994-day enterprise journey. Practitioners split on automation: GrowthSpree pushes Claude-driven outreach to 100 contacts, while Fullfunnel io warns that volume beyond capacity kills the program.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every serious operator gates ABM on deal economics before touching tactics. TK Kader lays out the fit test: a larger ACV, multiple decision makers and long sales cycles, and flatly says that for a self-service SaaS business where a user signs up and swipes a credit card, ABM 'might be overkill' [rH2rc9-LY00 @ 00:04:01]. AdConversion's Brandon Alysa Glue puts a number on it, roughly $20,000 ACV or more, or any contract that requires a CFO sign-off, and adds that if accounts are too small for title filters to work, they probably are not ABM-qualified at all [FPPnVM3_KPk @ 00:18:13]. Fullfunnel io sets its red-flag line higher for enterprise pipeline, listing ACV below 30K, an MQL-driven lead-gen focus, siloed teams, a 1,000-account list and an expectation of $1M in 30 days as red flags [glV72-awJAU @ 01:17:37]. Senator We Run Ads closes the low end entirely: ABM is not built for $2 to $10 per month tickets, and when it does fit, it deserves at least 25% of the media mix [Jx0muHw5NUY @ 00:13:30]. The shared logic is blunt: TK Kader calls ABM 'probably a little bit more expensive' than other motions, so it only pays where deal size justifies concentrated spend.

The second point of agreement is that ABM dies without sales and marketing operating as one unit, with leadership forcing it from the top. Craig Rosenberg of TOPO calls ABM 'a business decision' made top-down, with the VP of Sales and the CEO saying 'get us in... we got it,' and Sangram of terminus says pure marketing-only or sales-only efforts fail, pushing a single shared scorecard instead of 15 to 20 minutes of arguing over whose numbers are right [Co22pd-mVlk @ 00:39:16]. Sarah Challis is equally direct: if the sales team or senior management is not on board, 'it can be really hard to pull this off,' and marketing cannot run the strategy alone [nZS7xjR3bD0 @ 00:07:19]. Marketing Business Network describes the mechanics as an inverted funnel, where sales and marketing first agree on accounts by revenue potential and strategic fit [MNUNce5QMnc @ 00:00:44]. Fullfunnel io's diagnosis of failing programs lands in the same place, naming the absence of shared systematic planning with sales, where the only alignment is a list of territory 'biggest logos', as the first of five failure causes [glV72-awJAU @ 00:06:45]. Every operator here treats that alignment as the entry ticket, not a later optimization.

Practitioners also agree that the account, and the buying group inside it, replaces the lead as the unit of work, while demand generation stays switched on. Sangram puts it as 'we don't close leads we close accounts,' and Craig Rosenberg tells teams not to turn demand gen off ('the Titanic'), instead pivoting field events so 60% or more of the seats come from target accounts; that client grew pipeline 30% on 20% fewer leads [Co22pd-mVlk @ 01:03:22]. Rosenberg's replacement scorecard metric is TAP, target account pipeline. In Love With Marketing frames ABM as demand gen pointed at specific target accounts only, with the two sharing workforce, vendors, budgets and martech [CNTwxh9-1AI @ 00:02:38]. ATAK Interactive's Hannah Keeling uses the net-versus-spear image, says ABM breaks with 'a million accounts,' and argues the two run in tandem, with the only question being which lever to pull harder [FCu5IsBzx4U @ 00:03:46]. TK Kader warns against confusing ICP with TAM, citing a $12B TAM where the real ICP is a narrow slice, and says thousands of Dream 100 candidates mean the ICP needs refining [rH2rc9-LY00 @ 00:05:13]. The consensus target list stays short, strategic, validated against closed deals, and owned jointly by sales and marketing.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: TK Kader's five-step build runs in strict order. First comes an ICP fleshed out across 29 points of firmographic, demographic and technographic data; then messaging that spans email subject lines, the first sentence of a cold call, ad copy and homepage hero text; then a Dream 100 built in a spreadsheet or CRM with key contacts; then real personalization, which at Tower meant researching public quarterly filings rather than 'insert school' tokens [rH2rc9-LY00 @ 00:05:00]. Execution pairs sales outbound by email, DM and calls with marketing air cover from ads, organic social, SEM/SEO, intent tools and events, sized at 100 accounts times 5 people, or 500 contacts [rH2rc9-LY00 @ 00:11:24]. Skip steps one through four and hand an agency a 'napkin' ICP, Kader warns, and you burn your brand. Prospeo's Cole tiers the list in Sales Navigator by headcount, 1,000+, 200 to 1,000 and 1 to 200, saves each as a named account list, and runs lead search for titles like 'head of marketing,' remembering Sales Navigator shows only 25 accounts per page [OqdXhRy5QNY @ 00:02:08]. Senator We Run Ads expands lists with Leadfeeder website-visitor identification or a one-time manual Google search, and segments 2,000-account lists by size or revenue [Jx0muHw5NUY @ 00:03:58].

Fullfunnel io turns that sequence into an operating system. Accounts split into three sublists: a Cluster ICP of cold accounts getting awareness, a Future Pipeline that sales touches only after an agreed engagement threshold, taking about 20% of sales time, and an Active Focus list on fully personalized playbooks with weekly touchpoints [glV72-awJAU @ 00:38:59]. Each playbook ships with an outline, success criteria agreed with sales such as 20 accounts and 25 buyers, time required, templates, AI prompts and a plan B, while reps run a one-hour daily slot against a checklist and the whole team holds weekly meetings plus 5 to 10 minute daily stand-ups early on; the full stack runs under $1,000 a month with Goldcast, FullEnrich connected to Claude, and Apify scraping LinkedIn engagement weekly [glV72-awJAU @ 01:14:21]. Snowflake's Lars Kristensen scores engagement in Engagio at 2 points per site visit, plus 2 for a high-value page, 10 for a white paper, 15 for a webcast and 30 for a physical event, then seeds new AE territories with the most-engaged accounts [Co22pd-mVlk @ 01:35:55]. Offers escalate by stage, from a dummies guide for unaware accounts to a live demo for engaged ones and a free trial for highly engaged ones.

Paid and outbound mechanics come with hard settings. Prospeo's LinkedIn ad build uses a lead-gen objective with an uploaded company list, which needs at least 300 valid contacts and 24 to 48 hours of processing before targeting goes live, narrowed by job title and run as warm-up, cover and wake-up ads; outbound starts with email in LGM because of LinkedIn's weekly connection limits [OqdXhRy5QNY @ 00:08:12]. Aqil Jannaty budgets 5,000 to 10,000 a month for LinkedIn awareness ads despite high CPMs, calls ZoomInfo very expensive, and favors a B2B podcast play where the prospect is invited on as a guest, warmed up on an intro call, and the content is repurposed [sYgF5NyLeo8 @ 00:07:18]. AdConversion reports that at Thought Industry a Google Ads question keyword, 'LXP vs LMS,' cost pennies on the dollar against roughly $75-a-click target keywords, with the next-closest campaign's cost per lead 123% higher [FPPnVM3_KPk @ 00:25:10]. On the AI side, GrowthSpree runs Claude co-work on the Pro plan or above plus the Chrome extension to pull ICP-matched people from a LinkedIn company page, research posts and company news, write a personalized drip for 100 contacts, and send the connection requests [gq_DLeTobXo @ 00:03:39].

callout.title: Field-Tested Accelerators From the Operators
callout.body: Four plays the practitioners use to pull open opportunities and cold accounts forward faster than standard ABM sequencing.
items: Run objection-acceleration campaigns: ask sales for their top 10 objections and target the open-opportunity list with ads answering each one, such as accounts 'concerned about price' [AdConversion — FPPnVM3_KPk @ 00:06:48].
Fire pre-SDR campaigns 2 days to 2 weeks before outreach; at the CPG client this lifted connect rates, meetings and target account pipeline [LinkedIn for Marketing — Co22pd-mVlk @ 01:00:37].
Mine job changes: champions who changed jobs carry a 114% higher win rate per UserGems, and 70% of budget decisions happen in a buyer's first 100 days [AdConversion — LbEgZ7SpArs @ 00:02:02].
Work the buying committee bottom-up through Relationship Explorer, then reference those conversations when you reach the VP [Prospeo — OqdXhRy5QNY @ 00:03:49].

sop_steps.title: Qualify Fit and Plan Jointly
sop_steps.action: Confirm ACV and buying-committee fit, then lock sales and marketing into a one-to-three-day planning session.
sop_steps.detail: Run closed-won analysis on the highest-ACV and fastest deals, use lost deals for disqualification criteria, and match account count to team capacity [Fullfunnel io — glV72-awJAU @ 00:24:14].

sop_steps.title: Build and Tier the Account List
sop_steps.action: Split 'could buy' from 'likely to buy now' and concentrate budget on the smaller list.
sop_steps.detail: Ask your best reps who belongs on it or mine the CRM; targeting 10 to 20 companies is fine when 5 to 10 accounts would otherwise eat the budget [AdConversion — LbEgZ7SpArs @ 00:01:00].

sop_steps.title: Map Personas and Messaging Pillars
sop_steps.action: Strip non-buyers from targeting and build messaging pillars for decision makers and influencers.
sop_steps.detail: Exclude accounting, admin and HR, separate decision makers (CEO, procurement) from influencers, and build pillars on testimonials, USPs and pricing, and ease of migration and support [Senator We Run Ads — Jx0muHw5NUY @ 00:05:50].

sop_steps.title: Launch With Air Cover and a Monday Metrics Loop
sop_steps.action: Run sales outbound under ads, social and events, then review results weekly as one team.
sop_steps.detail: Hold a Monday sales and marketing meeting tracking campaign to opportunity to customer, diagnose ICP, then messaging, then channel, and double down on the one channel that crushes it [TK Kader — rH2rc9-LY00 @ 00:15:10].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first fight is over who owns the target account list. Sangram of Terminus tells marketers to be brave and build the list themselves instead of waiting for sales, because companies hire Account Executives, not lead executives [Co22pd-mVlk @ 00:15:41]. Aqil Jannaty reverses that split: sales builds the list, marketing builds the channels, and the starting unit is about 100 dream companies with mapped buying committees, ranked line by line with AI [sYgF5NyLeo8 @ 00:01:51]. Size is the second fault line. Lars Kristensen at Snowflake runs 3,000 target accounts and 200 one-to-one accounts with only two ABM staff. That list came from pushing 25,000 accounts through ICP mapping and letting each of about 50 reps pick roughly 60 [Co22pd-mVlk @ 01:32:09]. Fullfunnel io treats 1,000 accounts as a red flag on its own, alongside ACV below 30K, a lead-gen MQL focus, siloed teams, and an expectation of $1M in 30 days [glV72-awJAU @ 01:17:37]. Fullfunnel's own planning checklist ties account count to team capacity. Snowflake's 3,000 also sits on top of a far smaller one-to-one core of 200. Match the count to the people actually running the plays, then expand once the core is producing.

Automation splits the room hardest. GrowthSpree runs the entire outreach motion through Claude co-work and the Claude Chrome extension with no other automation tools. It builds the persona list from LinkedIn company pages, researches posts, comments and company news, and writes a personalized LinkedIn drip. It then scales from one prospect to all 100 contacts, with separate primary and secondary ICP sequences [gq_DLeTobXo @ 00:03:18]. Fullfunnel io pushes the other way. It warns that volume beyond team capacity will kill the program and that accounts which have never engaged get no sales pitch, because if they don't know us, probably they're not going to buy from us. Its Active Focus sublist gets fully personalized playbooks and weekly touchpoints, while cold Cluster ICP accounts get awareness only [glV72-awJAU @ 00:39:16]. Personalization depth is the second split. TK Kader says inserting a school name is not personalization; at Tower the team researched public quarterly filings before touching an account [rH2rc9-LY00 @ 00:09:47]. Aqil Jannaty argues that overpersonalization is killing ABM. The better move, in that view, is finding the watering holes where each persona actually spends time, and Aqil notes that security buyers are closed to cold email entirely [sYgF5NyLeo8 @ 00:05:23].

On demand generation, nobody fully agrees. Aqil Jannaty dismisses it as spray and pray [sYgF5NyLeo8 @ 00:00:54]. Craig Rosenberg of TOPO gives the opposite tip number one: don't turn it off, because it is the Titanic. Rosenberg instead pivots field events so 60%+ of the seats come from target accounts, a move that grew pipeline 30% on 20% fewer leads [Co22pd-mVlk @ 01:03:22]. Hannah Keeling at ATAK Interactive refuses to pit the two against each other at all. In that framing demand gen is the net and ABM is the spear, and companies start with demand gen because it is quicker, then shift to ABM as they find their niche [FCu5IsBzx4U @ 00:04:30]. Paid media and tooling draw the same split. Aqil budgets 5 to 10,000 a month for LinkedIn ads, and Senator We Run Ads wants at least 25% of the media mix in ABM. Fullfunnel io, by contrast, calls ads a quantity distribution channel and runs its full stack for under $1,000 a month [glV72-awJAU @ 01:32:34]. Terminus runs 20+ tools and Snowflake about 25, with Snowflake piping everything into its own data warehouse. Craig Rosenberg's rule holds either way: strategy first, tech stack second.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The cheapest failure to avoid is running ABM on a business that cannot carry it. TK Kader calls ABM probably a little bit more expensive than other motions. A self-service SaaS where users sign up and swipe a credit card might find it overkill, because fit needs a larger ACV, multiple decision makers and long sales cycles [rH2rc9-LY00 @ 00:04:01]. Brandon Alysa Glue on AdConversion puts the floor at about a $20,000 ACV, or any contract that requires a CFO sign-off. Glue adds that accounts too small for title filters are likely not ABM-qualified [FPPnVM3_KPk @ 00:18:13]. Fullfunnel io sets its red line higher and flags ACV below 30K as a reason to walk away [glV72-awJAU @ 01:17:37]. Senator We Run Ads rules out $2 to $10 a month tickets entirely [Jx0muHw5NUY @ 00:13:30]. Hannah Keeling adds the account-count version of the same check: ABM fails with a million accounts, and if you cannot identify targets or align sales and marketing, you are a demand-gen client. Sarah Challis supplies the budget sanity check for teams that clear the bar. Spend roughly 5% of deal value, which is £5,000 against a 100K deal, and do not get crazy ambitious relative to what the company is doing now.

The second trap is a clock that does not match the sales cycle. A Fullfunnel io client demanded $3M from a pilot within three months on a 15-month cycle, while Fullfunnel's own tracking shows 994 days from the first touchpoint to engagement [glV72-awJAU @ 00:24:14]. Their webinar poll found nobody rating ABM great, about 60% so-so and 40% frustrated. Short-term conversion playbooks and missing leading or lagging indicators were among the five causes they named. Russell Prue at AdConversion watched a client burn most of the budget on 5 to 10 accounts. Meanwhile, the list sales actually cared about for the next 3 to 6 months got only 20 to 50 impressions in 90 days [LbEgZ7SpArs @ 00:01:00]. Prue's diagnostic is blunt. No impressions means fixing distribution, no engagement means fixing content, and sales saying not sure at two months is a red flag [LbEgZ7SpArs @ 00:08:08]. Rob on the LinkedIn panel warns against buying programmatic before the list, database and sales orchestration are built, since that invites ROI questions that tarnish the whole initiative [Co22pd-mVlk @ 02:17:30]. Fullfunnel also refuses to chase early budget increases, because asking puts the gun in front of your head.

The ugliest failures happen at the moment of contact. TK Kader warns that skipping the ICP, messaging, Dream 100 and personalization steps and handing a napkin ICP to an agency or fractional CMO will burn your brand. A weak first impression earns the reply: we went with the other guy [rH2rc9-LY00 @ 00:13:24]. The LinkedIn panel catalogued what this looks like on the receiving end. Rob was told we sell to e-commerce companies like you despite running a B2B tech company. Matt received cupcakes with no sender name and a pizza box holding only a glossy sheet. Tai got a marshmallow fluff jar captioned last fluff you'll ever get from us [Co22pd-mVlk @ 01:52:08]. Matt's rule is that gifts sent to the wrong person just look like regular marketing with direct mail. The moderator's brother was hooked by a free-trial offer, but the telesales rep did not know about the trial and pushed an amazing deal today. The brother never bought, and the story spread among Seattle entrepreneurs, because you can't isolate those bad experiences anymore [Co22pd-mVlk @ 01:54:54]. Sarah Challis names the internal version: if sales or senior management are not on board, it is really hard to pull off [nZS7xjR3bD0 @ 00:07:19].

callout.title: Kill-or-Continue Gate Before Spending Another Dollar
callout.body: Run these four practitioner-reported checks before launch and again at the two-month mark. Any single failure is a reason to stop, reset the list, or fall back to demand gen.
items: Walk away if ACV is below 30K, the team is chasing MQLs, the list is 1,000 accounts, or leadership expects $1M in 30 days [Fullfunnel io — glV72-awJAU @ 01:17:37].
Treat sales saying not sure at two months as a red flag; diagnose no impressions as a distribution problem and no engagement as a content problem [AdConversion — LbEgZ7SpArs @ 00:08:08].
Do not ask for a budget increase to rescue a weak pilot, because that puts the gun in front of your head [Fullfunnel io — glV72-awJAU @ 01:23:19].
Audit any agency's list-building, demand clear outcomes such as 4 to 8 conversations a month, and treat revenue promises as a red flag [Aqil Jannaty — sYgF5NyLeo8 @ 00:14:12].

chapters.pull_quote: "We don't close leads, we close accounts." — Sangram, attributed to LinkedIn for Marketing (Co22pd-mVlk @ 00:14:02).
action_checklist: Run a closed-won analysis of your highest-ACV and fastest deals, plus lost deals for disqualification criteria, before picking a single account (Fullfunnel io, glV72-awJAU @ 00:24:14).
Split the list into could buy and likely to buy now, and start with the smaller in-market list of 10 to 20 companies (AdConversion, LbEgZ7SpArs @ 00:01:00).

Tier accounts with Tier 1 enterprise getting deep personalization from top reps, Tier 2 mid-market getting structured outreach, and Tier 3 small businesses getting automation (Prospeo, OqdXhRy5QNY @ 00:00:50).

Set leading KPIs (are accounts seeing ads, engaging, progressing) and lagging KPIs (meetings, pipeline, conversion against baseline) in a CRM report or Looker before launch (AdConversion, LbEgZ7SpArs @ 00:05:58).
Run pre-SDR campaigns 2 days to 2 weeks before outreach so marketing and SDRs hit target accounts together and lift connect rates and meetings (LinkedIn for Marketing, Co22pd-mVlk @ 01:00:37).
Hold a Monday sales and marketing metrics meeting, check ICP then messaging then channel, and double down on the one channel that crushes it (TK Kader, rH2rc9-LY00 @ 00:14:21).

chapters.question_prompt: Which personalized ABM and outbound approaches help open enterprise accounts and sustain engagement through long sales cycles?
chapters.title: Enterprise Account Plays: Gifting, Personalization, and Outbound
chapters.subtitle: Strategic gifting, direct mail, one-to-one ABM, phased rollouts, account-based experiences, enterprise sales cycles, and examples from LiveRamp, Ramp, Snowflake, and Hightouch
chapters.executive_summary: Enterprise account plays pay only where deal size carries the cost. Practitioners set the floor anywhere from roughly $10K a year to deals of 50,000-100,000 or more. They agree that sales capacity, not marketing ambition, sizes the list: Snowflake's Casey Patterson targets 10 of a rep's 100 accounts. Gifting works warm and fails cold. Alyce's Nick Bennett and Rocket SaaS both refuse cold sends, and Outgage calls gifting without follow-up a waste of budget. The numbers behind the mechanics are concrete. Steve Armenti's agent-researched executive experiences turned 11 of 30 contacts into meetings and a $1.3M result. Outgage's Wrike box drew 41% clicks. Ronen Pessar's re-scored phone list lifted the conversation rate from 1.6% to 39.6%. The main disagreement is over paid digital: Ramp is stopping paid-social ABM awareness, while Hightouch still reports lift by rotating creative every 2-3 weeks.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who put a number on enterprise account plays tied them to deal size, not company size. Sonish, a virtual CMO with about 15 years in the seat, runs a fit checklist that demands a limited addressable market, deals of 50,000-100,000 or more, sales cycles of 3-6+ months, persona-level personalization and POCs, and upsell potential. The checklist warns that thousands of target companies is not really ABM and that SMB or mass-focused SaaS should stay out [0Rhumt5MUDw @ 00:07:53]. Bev Burgess draws the same line from the other direction. Burgess has helped firms with fewer than 20 employees, because deals worth hundreds of thousands to millions justify the effort, while deals around 5,000 belong in targeted demand gen [Vdq5ROPgQzw @ 00:11:40]. George and Kevin at The B2B Playbook set the floor lower with the same logic: a $500 product cannot fund a $150-200K salesperson, so ABM starts paying off at roughly $10K a year and up [TMEMDzAg5QA @ 00:12:13]. Patience is the other shared prerequisite. Sonish allows at least 3-4 months before any movement in pipeline. Burgess expects leading indicators at 3 months, proofs of concept and invitations to pitch at 6, and a full year of testing, with outcomes doubling only once the program is embedded over 2-3 years [Vdq5ROPgQzw @ 01:03:48].

The second point of agreement is that sales capacity, not marketing ambition, sets the size of the list. Casey Patterson, who runs 23 ABM marketers at Snowflake, calls the sales team 'the bottleneck' and 'the deciding factor to the amount of accounts that you target.' If a rep owns 100 accounts, target 10, and expect meetings at 4 of them as the run rate [uWRminjpXsE @ 00:40:10]. Overloading reps backfires: 1,000 accounts producing 100 meetings for 2 reps just yields 'crap' meetings. On the Exit Five panel with Ramp and Hightouch, the caps get specific. Snowflake's Majors team runs about 20 accounts per ABMer, the prospect team runs roughly 40 reps at 2-3 accounts each for 120-150 total, and Brian caps Hightouch AEs at 20 accounts at a time [q_PvrQsWu-E @ 00:16:30]. Burgess sizes the human side the same way. A 1:1 marketer typically covers about 5 accounts, and a pilot should run 1:1 on 3 accounts or 1:few on clusters of about 15, budgeting roughly one day a week per account or cluster [Vdq5ROPgQzw @ 00:19:08]. LiveRamp's Ben pushed that discipline into the CRM itself, deleting non-target accounts from Salesforce and insisting 'it's worth it' [wQlrlFnnsuc @ 00:10:50].

On gifting, the consensus is blunt: never lead with it cold, and never send it without a sales follow-up. Nick Bennett, drawing on 7 years of gifting experience at Alyce, says 'you should never use gifting on like that first touch.' Sending 500 gifts to 500 cold accounts and hoping for conversion is 'not gonna happen,' while warmer accounts convert at 5-15% [4kdiiYL17XU @ 00:23:20]. Rocket SaaS applies the same rule to direct mail: 'I wouldn't do a cold direct mail campaign' [5XU6PUsdwEM @ 00:40:07]. The Outgage team tells operators to start with warm leads, to use intent data before committing to any high-dollar campaign, and to cut gifting entirely at the decision and negotiation stage [v0lXcZYhFXc @ 00:45:57]. Their sharpest warning is economic: 100 one-off gifts sent with no sales follow-up is 'a waste of your budget.' Gifting stays in the plan because of what it returns once those warm-first rules are respected. Outgage's channel audit found that direct mail delivered the highest engagement and ROI of every channel measured. Paola, an ABM agency practitioner and former head of marketing, calls direct mail 'gold' as long as it runs as part of a multi-channel orchestration strategy [Ny5ZaSzEbNI @ 00:20:47].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Steve Armenti's 1:1 executive-experience play is the most fully numbered mechanic on record. The premise is that executives are 'assaulted with AI-generated garbage.' Reported cold email reply rates have slid from 8% to 3%, and Armenti's own data shows roughly 0.3% positive replies [Mv1ZTzPcy5A @ 00:04:12]. Ronen Pessar's outbound audits land in the same place, with cold-email replies at 1-3% [dpDcjwreO8o @ 00:02:10]. The build runs on Claude Code plus Clay's MCP agents and skills, with a human validating the output. One agent studies each person across LinkedIn, Meta, Reddit, webinars, podcasts and YouTube transcripts. A second agent sources custom or boutique experiences. The deliverable is a contact-level brief covering insight, experiences and outreach plan. That research produced a private chef at 'Monica's' home; she booked a meeting 2 days later, and the play was repeated for 10 others. It also produced a 2-day yoga retreat for a CMO and 18 holes plus a new driver for an Arizona CFO. Start with a list 2-3x the contacts you want: roughly 90-something names yielded 30, and 11 of those 30 became meetings [Mv1ZTzPcy5A @ 00:07:56]. Offers went out manually from rep or executive inboxes, and opens and engagement ran above 50%. The play is expensive, but it returned about 10x ROI at $50-100k ACV for a $1.3M result [Mv1ZTzPcy5A @ 00:08:32].

The gifting mechanics that produce numbers share one trait: every send is wired to a follow-up trigger. Outgage's Wrike campaign shipped a locked acrylic candy box. At least 41% clicked the call-to-action, and the BDR cadence fired automatically on ship, deliver and landing-page visit events [v0lXcZYhFXc @ 00:28:35]. The Zendesk drone campaign hit 46% engagement, with the landing page qualifying leads through a demo or Calendly booking or a white paper. A global e-gift link for Natural Intelligence drew 71% redemption, with 54% replying to reps [v0lXcZYhFXc @ 00:37:23]. Rocket SaaS works the cheap end: a £5 Celebrations box led 1 in 10 recipients to book demos across about 5 campaigns, and £20 lunch vouchers go out through Preso [5XU6PUsdwEM @ 00:42:00]. Sendoso's CEO, Chris, describes the plumbing at scale. Smart Send replaces about 15 minutes of gift research with regional persona suggestions, and Pun Power writes the gift message. Send timing keys off intent, and smart delivery picks home versus office using IP data and posted content [9csglJ7L4oo @ 00:21:33]. Automated sends also fire off closed-won in Salesforce, with a campaign services team handling sourcing. The effort ceiling is lower than it looks; as the Outgage founder put it, 'I can add a personal touch for 500 people.'

The phone is where the outbound practitioners converge. Morgan Ingram worked with roughly 30 teams through the Sales Team Six program over 7 months. Cold calling was the number-one converting channel for 26 of them, across HR, IT, cybersecurity and marketing personas [KH5mI_MoF2s @ 00:03:45]. Ronen Pessar rebuilt the scoreboard around 'completions.' A completion means reaching the intended target rather than a gatekeeper or AI assistant, delivering a concise pitch, learning where the buyer sits in the cycle, and setting a next step or moving them out. The target is 15-25 completions per rep per day, against the 0-2 most reps log today. On one 2,245-number list, re-scoring with Phone Ready Leads (now TitanX) moved results from 1 conversation per 60 dials to 21 from 53: a 39.6% versus 1.6% rate, roughly a 23x lift [dpDcjwreO8o @ 00:08:10]. Anyone who answered once goes into a priority callback bucket, where 20-40% convert. Ingram layers a LinkedIn 'spider web' on top: comment on posts in your space, connect with 180-200 people a week against the 200 limit, and send voice notes and videos [KH5mI_MoF2s @ 00:11:02]. For face time, Rocket SaaS runs 12-seat breakfasts at about £15 a head against £60-100k annual deals [5XU6PUsdwEM @ 00:32:16].

callout.body: Small execution details that separated the sends and calls that converted from the ones that disappeared into the noise.
items: Send the offer manually from the rep's or an executive's own inbox, not a sequencer; Armenti's opens and engagement ran above 50% this way [Steve Armenti — Mv1ZTzPcy5A @ 00:08:16].
Trigger the BDR cadence on ship, deliver and landing-page visit events so rep outreach is timed to the gift's tracking signals [AI Marketers Guild — v0lXcZYhFXc @ 00:28:35].
Put anyone who answered the phone once into a priority callback bucket; 20-40% of those convert [Ronen Pessar — dpDcjwreO8o @ 00:09:06].
Research the buyer's 'five to nine' (what they are passionate about outside work) and gift to that, not to the job title [B2B Fusion — 4kdiiYL17XU @ 00:20:55].

sop_steps.title: Size the list to sales capacity
sop_steps.action: Count real rep meeting capacity, then pick the accounts.
sop_steps.detail: If a rep owns 100 accounts, target 10 and expect meetings at 4 of them [Exit Five — uWRminjpXsE @ 00:39:42]. Pilot 1:1 on 3 accounts or 1:few on a cluster of about 15, at roughly one day a week each [Growth Manifesto Podcast — Vdq5ROPgQzw @ 00:19:08].

sop_steps.title: Build a contact-level brief
sop_steps.action: Research each person, then source an experience that fits them.
sop_steps.detail: One agent mines LinkedIn, Meta, Reddit, webinars, podcasts and YouTube transcripts, and a second sources boutique experiences, with a human validating the output. Start from a list 2-3x the contacts you need [Steve Armenti — Mv1ZTzPcy5A @ 00:05:23].

sop_steps.title: Warm first, then send
sop_steps.action: Gift only after a prior touch, and verify the delivery address.
sop_steps.detail: Never use gifting on the first touch; warmer accounts convert at 5-15%, while cold blasts fail [B2B Fusion — 4kdiiYL17XU @ 00:23:20]. Verify the address before shipping [AI Marketers Guild — v0lXcZYhFXc @ 00:49:58].

sop_steps.title: Trigger follow-up and time-box the sprint
sop_steps.action: Automate follow-up on delivery events and run the play as a short sprint.
sop_steps.detail: Always fire an automated follow-up from the marketing automation system alongside the BDR cadence [AI Marketers Guild — v0lXcZYhFXc @ 00:30:19]. Time-box the play to 2 weeks and measure it on engagement, intent and product users [Exit Five — uWRminjpXsE @ 00:34:58].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Gifting timing is the sharpest split. Nick Bennett at Alyce has seven years of gifting behind him. He says gifting is never the first touch, and that firing 500 gifts at 500 cold accounts hoping for a 10 conversion is not going to happen. His warmer accounts convert at 5 to 15 percent [4kdiiYL17XU @ 00:23:20]. Rocket SaaS backs him from the budget side. They would not run a cold direct mail campaign, and their £5 Celebrations box booked roughly 1 in 10 demos across about five campaigns, with direct mail held back from cold lists entirely [5XU6PUsdwEM @ 00:40:07]. Outgage lands in the same camp, telling teams to start with warm leads and to use intent data before any high-dollar send [v0lXcZYhFXc @ 00:45:57]. Steve Armenti runs the opposite play. His targets are not hand-raisers. They are signal-based executives who get a private chef at home, a two-day yoga retreat, or 18 holes with a new driver. The experiences are sourced after AI agents built in Claude Code and Clay mine LinkedIn, Reddit, podcasts and webinars. Eleven of 30 contacts took meetings, engagement ran above 50 percent, and the play returned roughly 10x at $50k to $100k ACV [Mv1ZTzPcy5A @ 00:09:27]. Armenti's list was 30 people; the warm-only camp is budgeting across hundreds.

Paid digital is the second fault line. At Ramp, Drew is stopping paid-social ABM brand awareness outright [q_PvrQsWu-E @ 00:17:31]. Brian at Hightouch only partly agrees. A digital-only treatment arm still showed lift, but target accounts see the ads around 300 times a day, so his team swaps creative every two to three weeks [q_PvrQsWu-E @ 00:18:52]. George and Kevin at The B2B Playbook watched LinkedIn's dynamic name-and-title ads lift CTR at first, then fade once everyone adopted them. George calls hyper-personalized digital normally overkill and pushes budget toward live conversations instead: gifts, podcast invites, co-hosted webinars and roundtables [TMEMDzAg5QA @ 00:25:48]. Casey Patterson runs 23 ABM marketers at Snowflake, and she goes further: ABM is not running digital ads at a set of accounts. Dave Gerhardt labels that framing the lie ABM vendors told the market [uWRminjpXsE @ 00:36:30]. Casey's own one-account play still stacked billboards and geo-fenced ads on top of other layers: an on-site hands-on lab, gifting follow-up and an SDR email sequence. Users of Coco inside the account doubled. In her playbook, ads are one layer of a two-week sprint with sales, measured on engagement, intent and product users rather than on clicks.

List size splits practitioners by an order of magnitude. Rocket SaaS tells SaaS founders to aim for 200 up to 500 companies. They build the list with Crunchbase, Apollo, Sales Navigator, Clay and intent signals such as hiring, a new CMO or fresh funding [5XU6PUsdwEM @ 00:13:23]. Casey Patterson at Snowflake caps a majors ABMer near 20 accounts because one person cannot know 200 accounts intimately. Her prospect team runs about 40 reps at 2 to 3 accounts each, or 120 to 150 total, and Brian at Hightouch holds AEs to 20 at a time [q_PvrQsWu-E @ 00:15:48]. Bev Burgess goes smaller for a pilot. She spreads risk across three 1:1 accounts or one cluster of about 15, budgets roughly one day a week per account, and expects a dedicated 1:1 marketer to carry about five accounts [Vdq5ROPgQzw @ 00:19:28]. Paola on the Sunshine Coast puts the one-to-few sweet spot at 2 to 7 accounts for pilots. She argues that one-to-many programs across hundreds of firms, like MYOB going after 600, are not ABM anymore and behave like demand gen [Ny5ZaSzEbNI @ 00:09:39]. The sizing lens differs too. Casey works off what reps can actually absorb, while Rocket SaaS checks TAM, channel affordability and competitors before committing.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Gift logistics break in mundane ways. Outgage's field list includes chocolate shipped in the summer, a send that ended in a bomb-squad incident, and a two-parter that opened with an empty first box [v0lXcZYhFXc @ 00:42:06]. Their address-verification warning comes with a target address where no package had landed in five years, so the recipient record gets checked before anything ships [v0lXcZYhFXc @ 00:49:58]. The bigger leak is gifting with no sales motion behind it. In Outgage's words, 100 one-off gifts without rep follow-up is a waste of your budget. They always wire an automated follow-up from the marketing automation system and fire BDR cadences on ship, deliver and landing-page visit events [v0lXcZYhFXc @ 00:22:03]. Casey Patterson adds the brand trap: sending the cheapest swag or wasteful packaging [uWRminjpXsE @ 00:45:05]. Outgage cuts gifting once a deal hits decision or negotiation, keeps redemption questionnaires short, and A/B tests messaging and workflows. The wins they report carried that machinery. The Wrike locked acrylic candy box drove 41 percent CTA clicks with BDR triggers attached. The Zendesk drone send hit 46 percent engagement through a landing page that qualified leads via demo booking or white paper.

The economics check starts before the first send. Rocket SaaS spent about 10 grand on US ads and got a couple of crap leads, because messaging, pricing and case studies were still UK-only. Their fix is aligning sales and the deck before buying reach in a new market, and they warn that a Wynter survey at £5,000 to £6,000 is not cheap either [5XU6PUsdwEM @ 00:15:26]. The B2B Playbook draws the deal-size line bluntly: a $500 product cannot fund a $150,000 to $200,000 salesperson, and ABM starts paying off around $10K a year and up [TMEMDzAg5QA @ 00:12:13]. Bev Burgess says fit follows deal size, not company size. She has run ABM for firms under 20 employees, but deals around 5,000 belong in targeted demand gen instead [Vdq5ROPgQzw @ 00:11:40]. Her own clock runs 3 months to leading indicators, 6 months to POCs and invitations to pitch, and a full year of testing. Sonish at Aritic rules out SMB and mass-focused SaaS and sets the floor at deals of 50,000 to 100,000 with three-to-six-month cycles. He calls the approach investment heavy and tells buyers to expect at least three to four months before movement in pipeline [0Rhumt5MUDw @ 00:11:43].

The quietest killer is overloading or under-supporting sales. Casey Patterson warns that pushing 1,000 accounts that produce 100 meetings onto 2 reps yields crap meetings. She sizes lists off rep capacity instead, targeting 10 of a rep's 100 accounts with a run rate of meetings at 4 of them [uWRminjpXsE @ 00:39:15]. Nick Bennett at Alyce opened 70 percent of target accounts within a quarter and a half in early 2021. He then names the mistake: neglecting acceleration and sales enablement behind that opening. Alyce now runs one revenue organization under a CRO with a shared bonus structure [4kdiiYL17XU @ 00:12:43]. Time assumptions break too. Ben at LiveRamp planned around a 120-day opportunity life cycle that turned out closer to 240. His MQL-to-opportunity conversion sits at 7.9 percent against a 15 to 20 percent goal, and his stated regret is not formalizing cross-channel benchmarking sooner [wQlrlFnnsuc @ 00:20:04]. Paola traced one failed pilot to a single cause: no dedicated ABM owner. Her rule is to start small but not too small, show early wins, then scale [Ny5ZaSzEbNI @ 00:15:10]. Multi-touch attribution at LiveRamp, covering first touch, middle touch and opportunity-create, took years to win internal adoption.

callout.title: Pre-Send Kill Switches
callout.body: Every one of these checks traces to money or meetings a practitioner lost firsthand. Clear all four before a gift ships, an ad buy goes live, or a list hits the reps.
items: No gift goes to a cold account as the first touch; warm the account or confirm intent first [B2B Fusion — 4kdiiYL17XU @ 00:23:20].
No send ships without an automated follow-up from the marketing automation system and a BDR cadence tied to ship, deliver and visit events [AI Marketers Guild — v0lXcZYhFXc @ 00:30:19].
The target list is sized against rep capacity, because the sales team is the bottleneck and the deciding factor on account count [Exit Five — uWRminjpXsE @ 00:40:10].
Messaging, pricing and case studies are localized for a new geography before a single ad dollar is spent there [Rocket SaaS — 5XU6PUsdwEM @ 00:15:26].

chapters.pull_quote: "You're gonna send 500 gifts to you know 500 cold accounts and hope that you're gonna have a 10 conversion it's not gonna happen." — B2B Fusion (4kdiiYL17XU @ 00:23:04)
action_checklist: Start the pilot list at 2 to 3 times the contacts you want, then cut to 15 to 25 signal-based contacts before sourcing any experience [Steve Armenti — Mv1ZTzPcy5A @ 00:07:21].

Catalog the market with non-selling calls that capture incumbents, contract expiry and renewal dates, then focus spend on accounts in-market within 3 months [The B2B Playbook — TMEMDzAg5QA @ 00:14:21].
Delete non-target accounts from the CRM and require 2 responses for a target-account MQL versus at least 4 for non-targets [Dun & Bradstreet — wQlrlFnnsuc @ 00:14:01].
Re-score phone lists for intent, and call back anyone who answered once, because 20 to 40 percent of that bucket converts [Ronen Pessar — dpDcjwreO8o @ 00:09:06].
Research each stakeholder's five-to-nine passions on LinkedIn and social before choosing a gift, not just their job title [B2B Fusion — 4kdiiYL17XU @ 00:20:55].
Time-box one-account plays to a 2-week sprint with sales and measure engagement, intent and product users [Exit Five — uWRminjpXsE @ 00:34:58].
